tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement (szilard/benchm-dl keras_backend.md, environment in versions.txt) times CNTK 2.0 against TensorFlow 1.2.1 as Keras 2.0.6 backends on four GPUs; every quoted 1080 Ti figure and the 'about 2 to 4 times' LSTM summary are on the page. Not A: the page does not name its scripts (the inspiring minimaxir/keras-cntk-benchmark keras_cntk_benchmark.py is public, MIT, but its README states no CPU or versions) and no CPU model is given for any column.

corrections.caveats: Third-party 2017-era numbers on old software (TensorFlow 1.2.1, CUDA 8, cuDNN 5.1, CNTK 2.0), one GPU model per column, no variance reported, CPU not stated; the page says only that it was inspired by Max Woolf's benchmark, and its K80 column is copied from Max Woolf's blog; minimaxir/keras-cntk-benchmark (MIT, 26 stars) holds keras_cntk_benchmark.py but its README states no CPU model or versions, and benchm-dl (70 stars) itself holds no Keras-backend scripts (only cnn-mnist/). The win is confined to LSTM/RNN and small dense models; TensorFlow is faster on both CNN tests (MNIST CNN 4.7 versus 5.0 s per epoch, CIFAR-10 CNN 14.2 versus 24.2 s on the 1080 Ti), and on the K80 column FastText also favours TensorFlow (58.3 versus 69.5 s); the Keras Python layer sits between the benchmark and both engines. Accuracy is comparable across backends. The repository was archived by Microsoft on 2026-02-17 (read-only); the last code commit is 2020-03-31 and the README calls 2.7 (2019) the last main release. The HKBU dlbench study (arXiv 1608.07249, claims 5-10x over Torch and TensorFlow on CPU LSTMs) was seen only as a search snippet because arxiv.org and dlbench.comp.hkbu.edu.hk are blocked here, so its numbers are not recorded; the hclhkbu/dlbench repo README (MIT, 170 stars) has the harness but no results. CNTK's own README makes no speed claim against other frameworks.

notes: All claimed numbers match the 1080 Ti column of keras_backend.md; tier B kept as an independent measurement. Shortcomings to record: 2017 software, CNN workloads slower than TensorFlow (up to 1.7x), CPU model and exact scripts unstated, repo archived 2026-02-17. The category (autodiff-and-ml-kernels) is a wave 8 category filed here by the seed backfill; the baseline TensorFlow is itself a record in this same batch.

tier_reason: Third-party suite (Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf, scripts per framework in the repo, NVIDIA DeepLearningExamples commits pinned, CPU Xeon Gold 5118 and 4x8 V100 stated) lists NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 and stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 against NGC PyTorch and PyTorch 1.6.0; every quoted figure is in the report tables. Not A because the prebuilt containers' compiler and build flags are not stated and the compared ResNet AMP rows use different batch sizes (TensorFlow 224 after OOM at 256).

corrections.claimed_speedup: ResNet-50 v1.5 AMP, NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 with XLA (bsz=224) vs NGC PyTorch (table bsz=256): 1198.55 vs 802.9 img/s on 1 GPU, 8588.45 vs 6154.66 on 8, 14931.03 vs 11991.94 on 16, 29171.69 vs 22551.16 on 32 (about 1.49x, 1.40x, 1.25x, 1.29x, derived from page data); NGC TensorFlow without XLA still leads (945.18, 6903.42, 12021.09, 24734.22 img/s; about 1.18x, 1.12x, 1.00x, 1.10x, derived from page data). BERT-base AMP bsz=max (both bsz=96), NGC TensorFlow with XLA vs NGC PyTorch: 468.10 vs 462.35, 3559.8 vs 3287.12, 5960.14 vs 5426.07 and 11650.0 vs 10349.12 sentences/s on 1, 8, 16 and 32 GPUs (about 1.01x, 1.08x, 1.10x, 1.13x, derived from page data). At BERT AMP bsz=64 the result is mixed: 422.53 vs 444.51 and 3112.73 vs 3251.7 (PyTorch ahead on 1 and 8 GPUs), 5050.86 vs 4936.92 and 9409.20 vs 9331.72 (TensorFlow ahead by 1-2% on 16 and 32 GPUs). Stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 AMP ResNet-50: 1075.27 img/s (1 GPU) and 6898.00 (8 GPUs), above NGC PyTorch, but 9870.15 (16 GPUs) and 19314.31 (32 GPUs), below 11991.94 and 22551.16.
corrections.caveats: Mixed evidence, not a clean win. The suite is run by OneFlow (a competing framework that tops every table) and published in October 2020, so the numbers are six years old. The wins come from NVIDIA's NGC build of TensorFlow 1.15.2 with XLA plus AMP, not the stock tensorflow/tensorflow v2.3.0 tree, and are against NVIDIA's NGC PyTorch examples; XLA itself now lives in openxla/xla. Without XLA, NGC TensorFlow BERT AMP is far slower than NGC PyTorch (183.25 vs 444.51 sentences/s on 1 GPU, 5189.07 vs 9331.72 on 32 GPUs at bsz=64; about 2.4x and 1.8x, derived from page data). Stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 BERT is slower than NGC PyTorch in both precisions (DLPerf README: FP32 2244.38 at bsz=64 vs 3039.3 at bsz=48; AMP 4168.79 at bsz=96 vs 10349.12 at bsz=96 on 32 GPUs, about 2.5x, derived from page data). In FP32 PyTorch is faster almost everywhere: ResNet-50 bsz=128 NGC TensorFlow 362.44/2721.98/5099.42/9514.64 vs NGC PyTorch 367.29/2887.65/5716.79/10917.09 img/s, TensorFlow 2.3.0 9418.44 vs PyTorch 1.6.0 10021.29 on 32 GPUs; BERT FP32 bsz=32 NGC PyTorch leads at every scale, and at bsz=max TensorFlow leads only on 32 GPUs (3089.74 vs 3039.30). The stock PyTorch examples were not run with AMP. The ResNet AMP comparison pits TensorFlow at bsz=224 (OOM at 256) against PyTorch at 256. XLA vs no-XLA gains inside TensorFlow are TensorFlow-vs-TensorFlow and are not counted as a win over PyTorch. PyTorch is also listed (wave 12) with older numbers showing it 1.3-1.5x faster than TensorFlow 1.4-1.12 on other workloads, so the two entries carry opposite claims. Tier B, not A, because compiler and build flags of the containers are not stated and batch sizes differ between some compared rows. Google's own XLA blog post was not opened.

notes: All quoted figures are in reports/dlperf_benchmark_test_report_v1.md; corrections add the 16-GPU rows, the mixed BERT AMP bsz=64 table and the much slower no-XLA and stock-2.3.0 BERT rows. Shortcomings to record: win needs NVIDIA NGC build plus XLA plus AMP, PyTorch faster in FP32 and in stock TF 2.3.0 BERT, 2020 numbers from a competing framework's suite, container build flags unstated. Category autodiff-and-ml-kernels is a wave 8 category filed here by the seed backfill.

tier_reason: Independent third-party CI shootout (ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark, V8 v7 suite forked from mozilla arewefastyet, README snapshot 10/11/2026) shows Duktape Score 682/842/371 vs MuJS 435/522/339 on ubuntu/macos-arm64/windows; build recipe public (ahaoboy/duktape-build build.sh runs make on svaarala/duktape master, Makefile CCOPTS_NONDEBUG -Os). Not A: GitHub runner CPU model and compiler versions are not stated; B matches the wave 12 precedent for this suite (ChakraCore, njs, MuJS).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ubuntu and macOS: ahaoboy/duktape-build build.sh clones svaarala/duktape master and runs make, whose duk target builds with -Os -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-stack-protector -g -ggdb and configure options from util/makeduk_base.yaml (DUK_USE_FASTINT, but also DUK_USE_INTERRUPT_COUNTER, DUK_USE_DEBUGGER_SUPPORT and DUK_USE_SELF_TESTS enabled); windows: release 2.7.0 built with make -f Makefile.cmdline. MuJS is built by ahaoboy/mujs-build .github/workflows/build.yml with 'make release HAVE_READLINE=no' from codeberg.org/ccxvii/mujs (MuJS Makefile flags not read). Compiler versions not stated.
corrections.caveats: The project itself does not claim to be faster than any named engine: its README stresses portability and compact footprint, and QuickJS is clearly faster in the same table (ubuntu 1522 versus 682; quickjs-ng 800). The wins recorded here are only over MuJS and weaker engines (xst, goja, Boa, Jint) in a third-party CI shootout: one run per engine, no variance, runner CPU not stated, ubuntu and macOS build master (2.99.99) while windows runs release 2.7.0, and the scores drift between daily runs (other wave 12 verifiers read Duktape at 489/905/371 in the 10/5/2026 snapshot versus 682/842/371 on 10/11/2026), which is large next to the margins. The lead over MuJS comes mostly from Crypto and NavierStokes: MuJS wins RegExp on all three platforms (ubuntu 251 versus 184) and on windows also wins Richards, DeltaBlue, RayTrace and EarleyBoyer, so the windows total (371 versus 339) is thin. The Duktape build handicaps speed (-Os, interrupt counter and debugger support compiled in). Binary size: Duktape 370.4K versus MuJS 378.8K on ubuntu, but 431.4K versus 395.5K on macOS, so the size edge is not consistent. A 2015 Scriptorium run (r-lyeh-archived/scriptorium, AMD A10 3.8 GHz, Windows 7, VS2015 RC or VS2013, recursive fib) has Duktape at 9.544 s versus v7 at 51.940 s (about 5.4x, derived from page data) and Jim Tcl at 12.280 s, but far behind PUC Lua at 1.341 s and most other embeddable languages (rank 32 of 50). A JerryScript issue (#4386) peak-memory row (Duktape 582,240 KB versus QuickJS 5,523,792 KB) looks like an aggregate and was not used.

notes: Scores, versions and sizes match the 10/11/2026 README snapshot; MuJS is already verified in wave 12 (batch-98), so baseline_in_list is true. Shortcomings to record: not faster than QuickJS or quickjs-ng, thin windows margin with MuJS winning 5 of 8 sub-tests there, daily-run score drift, -Os build with debugger hooks, runner CPU unstated; the Scriptorium figures were confirmed on its README.
